title: How long can a Unitree G1 hold a building load before its motors overheat?
summary: buildbot-payload checks loads against each joint's peak torque. Motors can only hold a fraction of peak indefinitely, and no continuous rating for the Menagerie G1 was found, so this sweeps the continuous/peak ratio from 0.25 to 0.6. From the MuJoCo static torques at the stud-carry pose (0.3 m ahead of the feet, 0.6 m high), the waist pitch motor already sits at 0.54 of peak with empty hands, so with a continuous rating below 0.6 of peak nothing is sustainable there, and at 0.6 only 0.6 kg is: even a 3.8 kg stud takes the waist to 0.91 of peak and, with a first-order thermal model (loss ∝ torque<sup>2</sup>), reaches its limit in 0.14 thermal time constants at a ratio of 1/3. A 3.4 kg nailer at stud height reaches 0.76 of peak; one end of a sheet with a person exceeds peak. A pose search then finds the 0.91 is posture-specific: a 150-pose grid reaches 0.33 of peak with the stud held 0.15 m ahead and 0.7 m high (wrist pitch binding, no self-collision flagged, stud geometry not modelled), which is sustainable at any ratio of 0.4 or more. Static torques only; the thermal time constant and the continuous rating are unsourced, so only dimensionless hold times are reported; not a rated runtime.
lede: can a stock humanoid hold a stud for a minute? G1 static joint torques re-read against a swept continuous-torque fraction: the waist is at 0.54 of peak with empty hands at the carry pose and 0.91 with a 3.8 kg stud, so below a 0.6 continuous ratio nothing is sustainable (0.6 kg at 0.6) and a stud reaches the winding limit in 0.14 thermal time constants at 1/3. A 150-pose search finds a posture (hands 0.15 m ahead, 0.7 m high) at 0.33 of peak, so the 0.91 is not the floor.
